entities.name: Alfonso de Cartagena
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Alfonso de Santa María de Cartagena (c. 1384 – 1456) was a towering intellectual and political figure in 15th-century Castile, a prominent *converso* who rose to become Bishop of Burgos, a distinguished diplomat, historian, and prolific writer. Born into one of the most influential Jewish families in Spain, his father, Solomon ha-Levi, converted to Christianity in 1391, becoming Pablo de Santa María, Bishop of Cartagena and later Archbishop of Burgos. This familial trajectory positioned Alfonso at the nexus of religious, political, and cultural shifts, making him a crucial figure in the development of Castilian humanism and a vocal defender of the *conversos* against accusations of heresy and insincerity.

His career was marked by significant achievements in both ecclesiastical and secular spheres. As a diplomat, Cartagena represented Castile with considerable skill at the Council of Basel (1434–1439), where he eloquently defended the kingdom's right to precedence over England and Portugal, enhancing its international standing. His literary output was extensive, including the legal-moral treatise *Doctrinal de los caballeros* (c. 1435), a Castilian translation and commentary on Seneca's works, and the polemical *Defensorium unitatis christianae* (1449), a vigorous defense of the *conversos* against the discriminatory statutes of the *Sentencia-Estatuto* of Toledo. His historical work, *Anacephaleosis*, offered a universal history from the creation to his own time, demonstrating his profound engagement with classical and Christian intellectual traditions.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Alfonso de Cartagena was a pivotal figure in 15th-century Castile, whose intellectual works and diplomatic efforts significantly shaped Castilian humanism, defended *converso* communities, and elevated the kingdom's standing in European politics.
